title: UK Households Face New Cost of Living Crisis as Middle East Tensions Drive Up Energy Prices

body:
British households are bracing for another wave of cost-of-living pressures as escalating Middle East tensions push energy and food prices higher, raising fears of a renewed inflation crisis that could hit the UK's 1.8 million-strong Indian-origin community particularly hard.

UK inflation held steady at 3% in February 2026, already above the Bank of England's 2% target, but economists warn the situation could deteriorate rapidly. The National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR) forecasts that the ongoing conflict could push inflation to 4.1% by 2027, while the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) has warned that Iran-related hostilities alone could force inflation to 3% by year-end — a full percentage point above earlier projections.

The transmission channels are clear: disrupted oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) supply routes through the Middle East are driving up wholesale energy costs, which flow through to household bills, transport, and food prices. The Joseph Rowntree Foundation has called the situation a "2026 energy price crisis," advocating for a universal discounted block of essential energy to protect low-income families.

For Indian-origin households in the UK — many of whom run small businesses in retail, hospitality, and food services — the squeeze is twofold. Rising input costs for energy and logistics eat into already thin margins, while consumers pull back spending. British-Indian business owners in sectors like restaurants and corner shops have reported energy bills doubling compared to pre-crisis levels.

The UK government has responded with measures including a £150 reduction in the energy price cap, a 4% pay rise for 2.7 million workers, and frozen rail fares. However, critics argue these steps are insufficient for the most vulnerable households. Knight Frank analysts have warned that the crisis could ripple into the housing market, potentially stalling property values in areas with high concentrations of immigrant families who stretched to buy during the low-interest-rate era.

The situation resonates deeply with the Indian diaspora in the UK, the largest ethnic minority group in the country. Community organizations report increased demand for food banks and financial advice services, particularly among elderly Indian-origin residents on fixed incomes. The Hindu Council UK and Sikh Council UK have both called for targeted support for ethnic minority communities disproportionately affected by energy poverty.

With the Bank of England signaling it may need to raise rates further to contain inflation, mortgage holders — including many British-Indians who entered the property market in recent years — face additional financial strain. Economists warn that without a resolution to Middle East hostilities, the UK could face a prolonged period of stagflation that tests household resilience well into 2027.
author: Diaspora Desk
